claims.claim: Glycobiology is the study of the structure, biosynthesis, and biology of saccharides (sugar chains/glycans).
Glycobiology is fast emerging as a primary field of interest in biomolecular and biomedical research worldwide.

Sugars influence almost every aspect of cellular processes, including cell-cell interactions, adhesion, signaling, clotting, receptor binding, hormone regulation, embryonic development, and structural roles.
Simple sugars have a complex language possibly more complex than DNA due to unpredictability.
Many proteins require post-translational glycosylation (glycoprotein formation) to function properly.
Monosaccharides are carbohydrates that cannot be hydrolyzed into simpler carbohydrate units and are the basic structural units of glycans.
The glycome is the current population pattern of sugars in and out of the cell, in free or conjugated forms such as glycoproteins and glycolipids.
Glycans continuously change over time, making them challenging to study.
Glycan structures cannot be easily predicted from genetic code in the way protein sequences can.
More than half of human proteins have sugars conjugated to them.
Neurons do not use glucose as the primary source of energy; believing they do is a mistake.
Cognitive impairment occurs when plasma glucose falls to about 2–3 mM and levels below about 1 mM can cause confusion and coma with sustained deprivation.
Stroke injury is more extensive in patients with hyperglycemia or diabetes than in normoglycemic patients.
If glucose were the primary energy source, higher glucose should improve resistance/restoration after stroke rather than worsen outcomes.
Treatment with exogenous ATP in experimental ischemic stroke is associated with exaggerated ischemic outcomes and dangerous systemic effects.
When ATP is degraded to ADP or AMP, energy is absorbed rather than released.
Constant darkness increases AMP levels in blood.
Injection of exogenous AMP induces hypothermia and a hibernation-like condition in mice and rats.
High levels of AMP indicate decreased cellular energy state.
Tardive dyskinesia occurs more frequently in patients with elevated blood glucose levels.
Aerobic glucose metabolism proceeds via glycolysis to ATP and pyruvate, then pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle generating ATP and reducing equivalents.
Glucose is mainly a source of building blocks (e.g., adenosine, ATP, nucleic acids, glycans) rather than energy.
A continuous supply of both oxygen and glucose is vital for normal brain metabolic function including synthesis, synaptic transmission, ionic gradients, and integrity.
Because melanin can dissociate water to produce oxygen, oxygen is not essential since each cell can produce its own oxygen.
Molecular hydrogen (H2) is a crucial reducing factor for cellular energy supply.
Hyperglycemia does not change retinal lactate, pyruvate, and ATP in certain cited in vitro and in vivo models.
DG/FDG methods identify magnitude of functional metabolic activity but do not resolve cell-type-specific pathway contributions or specific energy-requiring processes.
Overall brain metabolic imaging cannot provide glucose metabolism at the cellular level.
Glucose transport into brain cells requires multiple GLUT isoforms and therefore requires additional energy.
GLUT1 and GLUT3 abundance increases region-specifically following chronic seizures.
Most cell surfaces are covered with a dense coating of sugars called the glycocalyx.
Monosaccharides can generate far more linkage variation than nucleotides or amino acids, yielding vastly more possible oligosaccharide structures.
Most well-characterized glycan biosynthesis pathways occur in the ER–Golgi–plasma membrane pathway with co- or post-translational modification during trafficking.
Glycosylation in the cytosol and nucleus is common, with O-GlcNAc among the most common intracellular glycoconjugates.
Melanin transforms light energy into chemical energy through dissociation of the water molecule.
Melanin is about a thousand times more efficient than chlorophyll at transforming light energy into chemical energy.
Chlorophyll dissociates water irreversibly as 2H2O → 2H2 + O2.
Melanin captures the entire electromagnetic spectrum from gamma rays to radio waves for energy conversion.
Melanin reforms water and generates four high-energy electrons per two water molecules via 2H2O ↔ 2H2 + O2 + 4e−.
Melanin releases chemical energy in the form of diatomic hydrogen and high-energy electrons distributed throughout the cell from perinuclear melanosomes.
Diatomic hydrogen does not combine with water.
The nucleus has neither mitochondria nor ATP.
Nuclear energy requirements are fulfilled by overlapping melanosome-derived energy spheres that concentrate chemical energy in the nuclear center.
ATP-based pathways are insufficient for glycosylation energy needs and ATP→ADP would absorb energy.
Glucose is a crucial building block for cartilage function in vivo and for chondrocyte nutritional requirements.
Because humans survive longer without food than without water, water must be a more efficient energy source than food.
Polyphosphate storage organelles (acidocalcisomes) occur across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes and may represent a universal organelle.
The genetic code is essentially the same in all known living organisms.
Origin-of-life models are displaced by a melanin-first scenario, including the possibility of melanin in space.
Greater melanin content corresponds to fewer mitochondria (up to 83% less) and about 30% lower respiration, reflecting metabolic differences between Black and White populations.
One cup of alcohol decreases light-to-chemical energy transduction for almost two weeks due to ethanol forming covalent bonds with receptors.
Lower suicide rates in sunny countries are explained by higher melanin-derived chemical energy reducing depression.
Black and White skin burn similarly, but melanin increases chemical energy and accelerates tissue recovery.
Higher melanin content implies higher tissue oxygen levels and explains less coronary obstruction in Black veterans with acute coronary insufficiency.

concepts.definition: Study of glycan (saccharide) structure, biosynthesis, and biological function.
Covalently linked monosaccharide chain attached to proteins/lipids or present as a free carbohydrate structure.
The set and distribution of glycans in a cell/tissue/organism under specific conditions.
Carbohydrate-rich coating on the cell surface formed by glycoproteins, glycolipids, and proteoglycans.
Attachment of glycans to asparagine residues of proteins in the secretory pathway.
Attachment of glycans to serine/threonine residues; includes mucin-type O-glycans.
Dynamic intracellular addition/removal of single GlcNAc residues on nuclear/cytosolic proteins.
Coexistence of multiple glycan structures at a given glycosylation site within a protein population.
Facilitative glucose transporters important for BBB transport (GLUT1) and neuronal uptake (GLUT3).
Tracer approaches measuring glucose uptake/phosphorylation as proxies for metabolic activity.
Lysosome-related organelle where melanin is synthesized and stored.
Proposed mechanism that melanin dissociates and reforms water to yield H2, O2, and electrons as cellular energy.
Acidic, polyphosphate- and cation-rich organelle described in many microbes; related compartments exist broadly.

logical_flow: Observation -> Glycans are ubiquitous, structurally complex, and dynamically remodeled in cells.
Inference -> Continuous remodeling and biosynthesis imply continuous chemical-energy demand.
Reinterpretation -> Glucose is treated primarily as a biomass/carbon-chain source rather than an energy source.
Clinical interpretation -> Hyperglycemia-associated harms and ATP/AMP intervention failures are treated as inconsistent with glucose/ATP-centered energy models.
Mechanism proposal -> Melanin is proposed to convert light into chemical energy by splitting/reforming water, yielding H2, O2, and electrons.
Physiological implication -> Oxygen becomes less essential and hydrogen/electrons become primary energy carriers; melanosomes distribute this energy intracellularly.
Extension -> The mechanism is used to explain nuclear energy needs, evolutionary origins (melanin-first), and population health differences linked to melanin content.
